payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The materials are anonymous benchmark identities, so the conclusions are phenomenological rather than claims about real molecular structures.

Observations

At the full charge (0.040 mol reagent in 0.080 L solvent), reaction conversion was generally high, but crystal recovery and particle quality separated sharply. Batch 1 (S0/C0, 360 K reaction) gave conversion 1.00, reaction yield 0.616, crystal yield 0.510, and purity 1.00, but its fines fraction was 0.989. Thus reaction formation and crystal purity were not the main limitations; almost all particles were below 20 µm.

Changing process history alone did not resolve this. Batch 3 used S0/C0 with more seed, extended aging, and a thermal cycle; it retained crystal yield 0.502 and purity 0.988 but had fines 1.00. Batch 4 omitted seed and used prolonged staged cooling/aging, yet gave yield 0.496 and fines 1.00. Batch 9 held near 300 K for ten long aging periods rather than cooling deeply; recovery fell to 0.400 while fines remained 0.973. These results show strong history dependence but no evidence that simple extra residence time, seed omission, or the tested thermal cycle can coarsen the full-load population enough to satisfy the fines limit.

Material effects were meaningful but did not overcome the concentration effect. In comparable full-load runs, S2/C0 in batch 5 gave reaction selectivity 0.539 and crystal yield 0.478, whereas S3/C0 in batch 6 gave selectivity 0.459 and crystal yield 0.349. Batch 6 reported a larger normalized size channel (0.101), but fines remained clipped at 1.00. Near the 20 µm threshold, independently noisy size and fines channels can appear inconsistent, so that isolated size value should not be treated as proof of compliance. Catalyst comparison under the same S0 crystallization schedule was clearer: C3 in batch 8 outperformed C2 in batch 7 in selectivity (0.622 versus 0.512) and crystal yield (0.516 versus 0.420), although both remained fines-dominated (0.998 and 0.983). Batch 2, using S1/C1, was poorer still, with selectivity 0.373 and crystal yield 0.302, but solvent and catalyst effects are confounded in that batch.

Dilution caused the decisive change. Batch 10 halved the reagent charge to 0.020 mol while retaining 0.080 L S0 and used a small seed dose. It gave reaction selectivity 0.736, crystal yield 0.432, purity 0.991, and fines 0.887. This was a substantial fines improvement, although still outside specification. At 0.010 mol reagent in batch 11, with catalyst scaled proportionally, the final crystals were very large by the assay channels (normalized size 0.393, approximately 98 µm d50) and fines were essentially zero, but seed-excluded crystal yield was zero. The observed solids were therefore consistent with retained or grown seed rather than meaningful recovery of newly formed product. Batch 12 used 0.005 mol reagent, proportionally scaled catalyst, a 0.0005 g seed charge, and a slightly colder final crystallization temperature of 285 K. It produced purity 1.00, fines 0.00, normalized size 0.425 (approximately 106 µm d50), and seed-excluded crystal yield 0.00836. Batch 12 was consequently the highest-recovery completed batch satisfying both imposed quality limits, although it remained far below the 0.10 feasibility target.

Interpretation

A useful coupling approximation is

n_crystal,target / n_reagent,0 = Y_crystal ≈ X · S_rxn · f_precip · f_isolation,

where X is conversion, S_rxn is chemical selectivity, f_precip is the fraction of target transferred into crystals, and f_isolation represents filtration retention. For example, batch 1 had X·S_rxn ≈ 0.62, close to its measured reaction yield of 0.616, but only 0.510 appeared as seed-excluded crystals. In batch 11, conversion was 0.928 and reaction yield was 0.611, yet crystal yield was zero: substantial target existed, but the diluted liquor and 290 K endpoint apparently did not drive significant net precipitation. This demonstrates that optimizing the reaction alone is insufficient.

The crystallization trends are consistent with supersaturation control. With σ=(C−C*)/C*, nucleation commonly has a much steeper dependence on supersaturation than growth, schematically

J ≈ J0 exp[−B/(ln(1+σ))²],     G ≈ kg σ^g.

At full loading and deep cooling, high supersaturation would create many nuclei or secondary fines faster than existing particles could grow, explaining the high recoveries but fines fractions near one in batches 1 and 3–9. Dilution lowers σ and can suppress nucleation disproportionately, allowing a small number of seed particles to grow large. The transition was extreme: batch 10 still precipitated considerable product but failed the fines limit, whereas batch 11 crossed into an effectively seed-only regime. Batch 12 recovered only a small amount because its colder endpoint supplied slightly more driving force.

A population-balance representation is also useful:

∂n(L,t)/∂t + ∂[G(L,t)n(L,t)]/∂L = B_nuc δ(L−L0) + aggregation − breakage − loss.

The constrained observable is F20=∫₀²⁰ n(L)dL / ∫₀∞ n(L)dL, while the reported normalized size is approximately min(d50/250 µm,1). Because F20 is number-weighted, even a modest mass of large crystals can coexist with an unacceptable number of fine particles. This explains why good mass recovery did not imply acceptable particle quality.

Crystallization also purified the product strongly. Full-load reaction selectivities were often only 0.46–0.62, yet isolated crystal purities were usually 0.97–1.00. The target evidently had a favorable solid/liquid partition relative to byproducts under the tested conditions. The high purity therefore reflects selective solid formation, not necessarily intrinsically clean reaction chemistry.

Revisions and uncertainty

The experimental strategy was revised from full-load feasibility (batch 1), through seed-dose, aging, thermal-cycle, solvent, and catalyst tests (batches 2–9), to concentration control (batches 10–12). The first revisions established that additional aging and the tested thermal cycles did not cure full-load fines. The later dilution series revealed that supersaturation/loading was the dominant control variable.

The unresolved tradeoff is severe: high recovery at 0.020–0.040 mol charge produced excessive fines, while specification-compliant batches at 0.010 mol or below produced zero or very low seed-excluded recovery. Batch 12 is therefore a constraint-feasible recommendation, not a satisfactory optimization endpoint. Its measured recovery is also close enough to zero that assay noise and run-to-run process variation are important.

Untested alternatives include finely interpolating the charge between 0.010 and 0.020 mol, scaling catalyst proportionally, and mapping final temperatures between 285 and 290 K. That narrow region may permit meaningful precipitation without the nucleation burst seen in batch 10. Seed size distribution, seed addition temperature, gentler endpoint ramps, and controlled dissolution of fines followed by regrowth are also plausible levers, but the tested seed omission and thermal cycle did not establish their benefit. These are hypotheses for future study, not demonstrated mechanisms.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- Full-loading processes gave useful seed-excluded recovery but unacceptable fines. Batch 1 produced crystal yield 0.510 and purity 1.00, but fines were 0.989. Batches 3–9 likewise had crystal yields of about 0.35–0.52 and fines of 0.973–1.00. This directly supports the stated recovery/particle-quality tradeoff.
- Crystallization delivered high purity despite only moderate reaction selectivity. For example, batch 1 had reaction selectivity 0.619 but crystal purity 1.00; batch 6 had selectivity 0.459 and purity 0.966. Selective incorporation or rejection of impurities is a reasonable interpretation, although the measurements do not directly identify where each impurity went.
- Loading had a much larger apparent effect on particle quality than the tested material changes. Batch 10 at 0.020 mol reagent gave yield 0.432 and fines 0.887; batch 11 at 0.010 mol gave essentially zero seed-excluded yield and fines near zero; batch 12 at 0.005 mol gave yield 0.0084 and fines zero. By contrast, the full-loading solvent/catalyst screen in batches 2 and 5–8 never approached the fines specification.
- The tested full-loading aging, seed, and thermal-history changes did not solve the fines problem. Batch 3 used extensive aging and a thermal cycle, batch 4 omitted seed, and batch 9 aged for a long time near 300 K; all remained strongly fines-dominated.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple claim that longer residence or thermal cycling necessarily converts fines into large product crystals is contradicted by batches 3, 4, and 9. Those histories did not produce specification-compliant particles, and batch 9 lost recovery without a corresponding fines solution.
- A claim that material selection alone can solve the quality constraint at full loading is contradicted within the tested set: S1, S2, S3, C2, and C3 variants in batches 2 and 5–8 all failed the fines limit.
- The report treated dilution as the dominant causal variable, but that inference is stronger than the experimental design warrants. Batch 10 also had a different catalyst/reagent ratio from batches 11–12, and batches 10–12 used different cooling endpoints. The loading trend is real; its precise causal attribution is not isolated.

Still untested or interpretive:
- The proposed supersaturation–nucleation mechanism is consistent with the endpoints but was not directly measured. No time-resolved nucleation rate, solubility curve, mother-liquor concentration trajectory, aggregation rate, or breakage rate was obtained.
- The sharp transition between 0.010 and 0.020 mol reagent remains unmapped. It is unknown whether it is a smooth concentration response, a metastable-zone threshold, or partly stochastic.
- The suggestion that batch 12 recovered slightly more than batch 11 because of its colder endpoint is not causally established: reagent loading was also halved.
- Seed size distribution, seed addition temperature, and reproducibility near the apparent threshold remain untested.

2. One additional experiment

I would run 0.010 mol reagent in 0.080 L S0 with 0.00125 mol C0 and 0.001 g seed, reproducing batch 11 upstream. I would measure HPLC immediately before quenching, cool slowly to 290 K and measure particle size, then continue to 285 K and 278 K with particle-size measurements after each hold, followed by filtration and final assay. The intermediate measurements are non-destructive and make this a single batch with a resolved trajectory.

This experiment would distinguish three explanations:
- Insufficient cooling in batch 11: if seed-excluded yield becomes appreciable only after cooling below 290 K while size remains large and fines stay below 0.50, the low batch-11 recovery was mainly an endpoint/solubility problem.
- An unavoidable nucleation threshold: if recovery rises after deeper cooling but fines abruptly rise above 0.50 and size falls, the unresolved tradeoff is caused by crossing a supersaturation threshold.
- Insufficient target formation or an intrinsically seed-only dilute regime: if pre-quench HPLC shows low target formation, or if deep cooling still gives negligible seed-excluded yield while the seeded particles remain large, the limitation is upstream chemistry or insufficient available solute rather than the 290 K endpoint.

A particularly informative result would be moderate yield above 0.10 with fines below 0.50 at 285 K; that would falsify the pessimistic conclusion that the explored recovery/quality tradeoff is unavoidable. Conversely, a fines surge between 290 and 285 K would strongly support the nucleation-threshold interpretation.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The observation used least effectively was batch 6’s combination of normalized crystal size 0.101 with fines reported as 1.00. I largely dismissed this as independent channel noise near the 20 µm boundary. That was plausible, but incomplete: it could also indicate a broad or bimodal population, clipping, or disagreement between assay summaries. The raw particle-size artifact or a replicate measurement would have been more informative than treating the size channel as merely anomalous.

The least reliable held-out prediction is Q08, the cool–reheat–recool thermal-history case. Its outcome depends on a non-monotonic balance among dissolution of fines, dissolution of product mass, Ostwald ripening, renewed nucleation, and reaction-product solubility. Batch 3 provided only weak negative evidence because it used a different solvent/catalyst/loading regime and a different thermal cycle. I therefore had little matched evidence for the predicted reduction in fines, and even the direction of the yield change is uncertain. Q11 is also uncertain because it lies near the observed loading transition, but Q08 requires the larger mechanistic extrapolation.

payload.rationale: Q01/Q02: solvent S3 is expected to reduce recovery relative to S1 but modestly increase characteristic size; both remain fines-limited. Q03/Q04: the larger seed charge supplies more particles and surface area, giving slightly greater recovery but smaller number-weighted size and more fines. Q05/Q06: staged cooling should moderate the nucleation burst compared with immediately cooling to 278.15 K, so Q05 is coarser and less fines-rich, while Q06 recovers slightly more. Q07/Q08: the 300 K thermal excursion may dissolve preferentially small crystals and permit coarsening on recooling, but prior full-loading thermal cycling did not establish a reliable specification-level benefit; its interval therefore spans the fines threshold. Q09/Q10: another four hours at 278.15 K should add modest deposition and growth, slightly increasing yield and size, without curing the fine population. Q11/Q12: loading is the strongest lever. Lower loading suppresses nucleation and produces coarser particles but risks little seed-excluded precipitation; higher loading raises recovery while driving fines close to unity. All recipes contain seed, so particles are expected even when seed-excluded recovery is low. Purity is predicted to remain high because crystallization previously rejected reaction byproducts effectively. Uncertainty is widest near the sharp loading and thermal-history transition, especially for Q08 and Q11.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Best constraint-feasible completed batch: crystal purity 1.00 and fines fraction 0.00, with the highest observed seed-excluded crystal yield among feasible batches (0.0084); no batch met the 0.10 feasibility target while satisfying both quality limits.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The campaign supports a coupled reaction–crystallization mechanism in which chemical production and crystal quality are controlled by different, sometimes opposing, variables. Crystal purity was usually high once solids formed, but high product inventories produced excessive secondary nucleation and fines. The recommended batch 12 best balanced these effects.

Observed material effects

Catalyst C1 was used throughout, so the experiments establish a process for C1 but do not experimentally rank C0, C2, or C3. C1’s high nominal activity was consistent with the rapid reaction: in batch 12, 0.005 mol C1 with 0.016 mol reagent reached final conversion 0.964 after heating at 370 K for 900 s. Its final selectivity and liquid-phase yield were 0.817 and 0.808. Any claim that C1 is globally optimal would be untested.

Solvent choice affected both recovery and particle formation. At otherwise similar high-temperature reaction and staged-cooling conditions, S2 in batch 5 gave crystal yield 0.537, whereas S1 in batch 6 gave 0.439. This is consistent with the nominal lower solubility and higher growth tendency of S2. However, both high-loading batches had unacceptable fines: 0.984 for batch 5 and 1.000 for batch 6. S1 produced a larger normalized crystal-size signal in batch 6 (0.099 versus 0.054 in batch 5), suggesting less severe nucleation or better growth, although the comparison is not replicated. S1 subsequently enabled feasible fines at reduced loading in batches 7 and 12.

Reaction mechanism and time–temperature effects

A useful lumped scheme is

A → P,  A → I,  P → D,

where P is the crystallizable target, I represents competing byproducts, and D represents degradation. A simple kinetic approximation is

X(t) = 1 − exp[−(kP + kI)t],

with early selectivity approximately kP/(kP+kI), followed by loss if P undergoes degradation. The rate constants depend on catalyst, solvent, and temperature.

The observations favor a short, hot reaction over a long, cooler exposure for the conditions tested. Batch 1 used S2, 360 K for 3600 s and produced final selectivity 0.547 with degradation warning 0.156. Batch 2 used 330 K for 7200 s and gave selectivity 0.430 and degradation warning 0.207. Batch 3 at 320 K for 3600 s improved degradation warning to 0.093 but retained only 0.485 selectivity. In contrast, batch 5 at 370 K for 900 s gave selectivity 0.685 and degradation warning 0.045. Batch 12, using lower loading in S1 under the same nominal 370 K/900 s reaction, reached selectivity 0.817 with degradation warning 0.044.

Interpretation: rapid heating drives conversion before prolonged exposure accumulates impurity or degradation. This inference is mechanistically plausible but remains partly confounded by loading, solvent, and subsequent process history. The final-assay and preceding HPLC values also differed; for example, batch 12 HPLC reported conversion/selectivity/yield of 0.980/0.787/0.772, while the final assay reported 0.964/0.817/0.808. These differences reflect instrument noise and continued processing rather than a precisely resolved kinetic trajectory.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

The approximate target inventory entering crystallization scales as

nP ≈ nA,0 X S,

and the concentration driving crystallization as

ΔC(T) = nP/V − C*(T, solvent).

Crystal growth can be represented as G ∝ kgΔC, while secondary nucleation commonly rises more sharply, J ∝ kn(ΔC)^m with m > 1. Thus increasing target inventory can increase recovery but cause J/G to rise sharply, generating many particles below 20 µm.

The campaign strongly supports this nonlinear supersaturation interpretation. High-loading S1 batches gave high recovery but failed the fines constraint:

• Batch 8, 0.025 mol reagent and 0.005 mol C1: crystal yield 0.463, purity 1.000, fines 0.997.
• Batch 9, 0.020 mol reagent and 0.005 mol C1: yield 0.437, purity 0.982, fines 0.672.
• Batch 11, 0.018 mol reagent and 0.005 mol C1: yield 0.392, purity 0.975, fines 0.621.
• Batch 12, 0.016 mol reagent and 0.005 mol C1: yield 0.389, purity 0.992, fines 0.416.

The small loss in recovery from batch 11 to batch 12 was accompanied by a large improvement in fines, indicating a nucleation threshold rather than a smooth proportional response. Batch 12’s normalized size of 0.107 corresponds to a number-weighted d50 of about 26.8 µm under the declared size definition, consistent with its fines fraction falling below 0.50.

Purity behaved differently from particle size. Even batches with only moderate reaction selectivity frequently gave crystal purity near unity. For example, batch 5 had reaction selectivity 0.685 but crystal purity 0.979; batch 12 had selectivity 0.817 and purity 0.992. This indicates preferential incorporation of target into the solid and rejection of soluble impurities. Purity was therefore not the limiting attribute; number-based fines were.

Process-history dependence

Seeding, quench temperature, cooling path, and residence time affected the state from which crystallization began. The successful low-loading process quenched from the short hot reaction to approximately 319 K, added 0.05 g seed, cooled to 310 K over 14,400 s, held for 14,400 s at low stirring, cooled to 295 K over another 14,400 s, held again, and then filtered. This history allows seed growth before the lower-temperature precipitation step.

Initial revisions showed that simply extending or softening the crystallization was insufficient at high inventory. Batch 1 used 0.05 g seed, deep cooling to 260 K, and a long hold; it achieved crystal yield 0.474 and purity 1.000 but fines 0.989. Batch 3 cooled only to 295 K and held much longer, yet fines remained 1.000. Batch 4 used only 0.01 g seed plus a cool–reheat–recool cycle; its yield was 0.488, but fines remained 1.000 and normalized crystal size fell to 0.023. This argues that annealing cannot rescue a particle population after extensive primary or secondary nucleation, at least under the tested cycle.

Batch 10 also demonstrated that higher final temperature alone was not a reliable remedy. With 0.020 mol reagent and full C1 loading, its final crystallization temperature was 305 K rather than 295 K, but it still gave fines 0.981 and reduced yield to 0.345. Consequently, the successful revision was reduction of product inventory, not merely warmer isolation.

Development revisions

The campaign began with maximum reagent loading in S2 to establish conversion and attainable recovery. Those batches revealed excellent purity but nearly all-number fines. Longer holds, milder cooling, a lower seed charge, and a thermal cycle did not solve the problem. The process was then shifted to S1 and reduced reagent loading. Batch 7 first demonstrated feasibility: 0.020 mol reagent, 0.0025 mol C1, crystal yield 0.287, purity 0.997, and fines 0.396. Restoring the full 0.005 mol C1 increased reaction conversion and recovery but pushed batches 9 and 11 above the fines limit. Reducing reagent charge to 0.016 mol in batch 12 retained a yield of 0.389 while restoring acceptable fines at 0.416.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoff

The clearest unresolved tradeoff is recovery versus nucleation. The highest recoveries—0.537 in batch 5, 0.488 in batch 4, 0.463 in batch 8, and 0.437 in batch 9—were all infeasible because fines ranged from 0.672 to 1.000. Batch 12 is the highest observed recovery satisfying both purity ≥0.80 and fines ≤0.50. Its fines margin is 0.084, larger than the declared final-assay noise scale of 0.018, but process reproducibility was not measured because no recipe was replicated.

Other uncertainties include confounding among solvent, loading, catalyst ratio, and thermal history; unknown seed-size distribution; and fixed-world material residuals. Untested alternatives include intermediate reagent charges between 0.016 and 0.018 mol, other catalysts, different seed masses near 0.05 g, and alternative staged holds designed to increase growth without crossing the nucleation threshold. These could potentially improve recovery, but the present evidence does not establish that they would remain below the fines limit.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:

• A sharp recovery–fines tradeoff with target loading is the strongest result. Under closely related S1/C1 reaction and staged-cooling conditions, batches 8, 9, 11, and 12 used 0.025, 0.020, 0.018, and 0.016 mol reagent. Their crystal yields were 0.463, 0.437, 0.392, and 0.389, while fines fell from 0.997 to 0.672, 0.621, and finally 0.416. Thus batch 12 lost little recovery relative to batch 11 but crossed the fines specification. Interpreting this as a nonlinear supersaturation/nucleation threshold is plausible, although supersaturation itself was not measured.

• Crystallization strongly purified the target. Examples include batch 5, with reaction selectivity 0.685 but crystal purity 0.979, and batch 12, with selectivity 0.817 but crystal purity 0.992. Preferential target crystallization is an interpretation; the direct observation is the large difference between liquid-phase selectivity and solid purity.

• High recovery alone did not imply acceptable particle quality. Batches 4, 5, 8, and 9 produced crystal yields of 0.488, 0.537, 0.463, and 0.437, but their fines were 1.000, 0.984, 0.997, and 0.672. Batch 12 was the highest observed yield satisfying both specifications.

• S2 favored recovery, whereas S1 gave a larger size signal in the closest solvent comparison. Batch 5 using S2 gave yield 0.537 and normalized size 0.054; batch 6 using S1 gave yield 0.439 and size 0.099. Both failed the fines constraint, and this was only one unreplicated comparison, so it supports a solvent effect but not a universal solvent ranking.

• Simply extending or warming the crystallization did not reliably cure fines. Batch 3 had prolonged holds but fines of 1.000. Batch 4 included a reheat/recool cycle and also had fines of 1.000. Batch 10 ended at 305 K rather than 295 K yet gave fines of 0.981 and lower yield than batch 9. These directly contradict a simple claim that more time, annealing, or a warmer endpoint must improve the distribution.

Partially supported or confounded:

• The short, hot reaction appeared preferable to longer exposure. Batch 5 at 370 K for 900 s had selectivity 0.685 and degradation warning 0.045, versus batch 1 at 360 K for 3600 s with 0.547 and 0.156, and batch 2 at 330 K for 7200 s with 0.430 and 0.207. Temperature, duration, subsequent history, and sometimes crystallization conditions were not independently varied, so the proposed A→P, A→I, P→D scheme remains a useful interpretation rather than an identified kinetic law.

• The decisive variable may be target inventory n₀XS/V rather than reagent loading alone. Batch 7 and batch 9 both charged 0.020 mol reagent in S1, but batch 7 used 0.0025 mol catalyst and had liquid yield 0.624, crystal yield 0.287, and fines 0.396; batch 9 used 0.005 mol catalyst and had liquid yield 0.771, crystal yield 0.437, and fines 0.672. This supports an inventory mechanism, but catalyst concentration might also affect impurity identity or nucleation directly.

Still untested:

• C1 was never compared experimentally with C0, C2, or C3, so C1 optimality is untested.

• Seed-mass effects were confounded. Batch 4 used 0.01 g seed, but it also used a distinct thermal cycle; the 0.05 g batches therefore do not isolate seed mass.

• The proposed nucleation and growth relationships, J ∝ ΔC^m and G ∝ ΔC, were not measured directly. No supersaturation, nucleation-rate, growth-rate, or seed-size measurements were available.

• Reproducibility is unresolved because no final recipe was replicated. The final-assay noise scale does not cover batch-to-batch process variability.

2. One additional experiment

I would run one inventory-matching experiment between batches 11 and 12: charge 0.018 mol reagent in 0.080 L S1, use about 0.0035 mol C1, heat at 370 K for 900 s, measure the liquid by HPLC, then apply batch 12’s quench, 0.05 g seed, 310 K and 295 K staged cooling/holds, filtration, and final assay. The catalyst amount is chosen to seek approximately the same absolute target inventory as batch 12 while retaining batch 11’s initial reagent loading.

This would distinguish two explanations:

• If fines are governed mainly by target inventory/supersaturation, matching batch 12’s pre-crystallization target moles should give fines near batch 12’s 0.416, high purity, and approximately the same absolute crystal amount. Because the denominator is 0.018 rather than 0.016 mol, the fractional crystal yield would be expected around 0.35 rather than 0.389.

• If initial reagent loading, catalyst ratio, impurity composition, or another history-dependent variable controls nucleation independently of target inventory, the result should resemble batch 11 more closely: fines near or above 0.62 and crystal yield near 0.39.

The intermediate HPLC result is essential: if it fails to match the intended target inventory, the experiment would primarily refine reaction kinetics rather than cleanly test the crystallization explanations.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The account used batch 10 least effectively. It noted that the warmer 305 K endpoint produced lower recovery and much worse fines than expected, but the simple equilibrium/supersaturation equations did not explain that result. Batch 10 indicates that nucleation timing, seed survival, cooling trajectory, or an unobserved state variable matters—not merely final temperature and equilibrium solubility. That observation should have led to wider uncertainty for all thermal-history claims.

Q02 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It is the only solvent-S3 case, while no campaign batch used S3. Its prediction therefore depended almost entirely on nominal dossier properties, despite the explicit possibility of fixed hidden solvent residuals or misindexing. The simultaneous extrapolation to much lower solvent volume, much lower catalyst charge, 385 K reaction conditions, small seed mass, and deep cooling further compounds the uncertainty. Q08 is also weak because the sole thermal-cycle precedent, batch 4, was confounded, but Q02 has the largest unsupported material extrapolation.

payload.rationale: Q01, Q03, and Q05 are identical recipes and therefore receive identical predictions. For the solvent pair, S3 is expected to retain more target in solution, occlude more impurity, and support poorer growth than S1, reducing Q02 recovery, purity, and size while increasing fines. Increasing seed from 0.006 g to 0.05 g in Q04 should suppress some secondary nucleation and enlarge particles, but the high target concentration and deep 278.15 K endpoint are still expected to leave fines above 0.50. Staged cooling in Q05 should be less nucleating than the immediate deep-cooling history in Q06. The reheat in Q08 may dissolve some small particles and modestly improve size versus Q07, although the campaign's thermal-cycle batch showed that this effect is uncertain and unlikely to restore feasibility. The extra low-temperature growth period in Q10 should modestly increase recovery and size relative to Q09. Lower loading in Q11 reduces supersaturation and fines but increases the fractional loss of dissolved product; Q12 improves fractional recovery but is predicted to undergo extensive nucleation. Uncertainty is broad because these recipes use much less solvent and catalyst than the campaign batches, a smaller seed charge, a hotter and longer reaction history, and a deeper cooling endpoint. The intervals represent epistemic process uncertainty around noise-free outcomes, not final-assay noise.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 gave the highest observed seed-excluded crystal yield among batches meeting both constraints: crystal_yield 0.389, crystal_purity 0.992, and crystal_fines_fraction 0.416.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Observations

The reaction was generally driven to near-complete conversion, so catalyst/temperature mainly affected selectivity rather than conversion. With solvent S2, batch 1 (C1, 360 K) gave conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.534, and reaction yield 0.531. C3 at 345 K was similarly effective: batches 4–12 generally gave reaction yields about 0.537–0.552 and selectivities about 0.522–0.557. Under different thermal conditions, C0 and C2 were poorer: batch 2 gave reaction yield 0.422/selectivity 0.428, while batch 3 gave 0.414/0.388. Because catalyst and temperature were not varied factorially, this supports—but does not prove—that C3 is the best robust catalyst in the tested region.

Solvent S2 supported both strong reaction performance and substantial crystallization recovery. Replacing it with S3 in batch 8 reduced reaction yield to 0.465 and selectivity to 0.472; crystal recovery was 0.286, but fines remained 0.997. Thus S3 did not resolve the particle-quality problem. This is consistent with the nominal dossier: S2 has high relative growth, low nucleation tendency, low impurity occlusion, and lower solubility. The observed fixed-world response nevertheless shows that sufficiently deep supersaturation overwhelms those nominal advantages.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

A useful reaction approximation is

Y_target ≈ X × S_target,

where X is conversion and S_target is target selectivity. Since X was usually near one, improving reaction selectivity directly increased the maximum recoverable target inventory. Seed-excluded crystal recovery can be written

R_x = n(target in recovered crystals, excluding seed) / n(initial reactant),

with R_x bounded approximately by reaction yield. Crystallization also purified strongly: batches with meaningful recovery usually had crystal purity around 0.95–1.00 despite reaction byproduct signals around 0.30–0.37. I interpret this as preferential incorporation of target and rejection of reaction impurities. However, very pure, low-recovery batches can largely represent seed-dominated solids, so purity alone is not evidence of successful product recovery.

The central relationship was a sharp recovery–particle-size tradeoff. In S2, cooling deeply produced substantial recovery but extensive secondary nucleation. Batch 4, cooled to 298 K, recovered 0.368 but had fines fraction 1.000 and normalized size 0.0199, corresponding to a number-weighted d50 of about 5 micrometres. Batch 1, cooled to 285 K, recovered 0.428 but still had fines 0.989 and d50 about 17 micrometres. In contrast, warm endpoints preserved large particles but recovered almost no newly formed product: batch 5 at 302 K gave recovery 0.00735, fines 0, and d50 about 98 micrometres; batch 10 at 301 K gave recovery 0.00656, fines 0, and d50 about 94 micrometres.

This can be rationalized using supersaturation S=C/C*(T). A schematic kinetic model is

J = k_n(S−1)^m,
G = k_g(S−1)^g,

where J is nucleation rate and G is growth rate. If m exceeds g, a small decrease in temperature near the supersaturation threshold causes nucleation to rise much faster than growth. A population balance,

∂n(L,t)/∂t + ∂[G n(L,t)]/∂L = B(t)δ(L−L0),

then explains why the number fraction below 20 micrometres can approach one even when appreciable crystal mass is recovered. The reported fines metric is number-weighted, so a large population of tiny secondary crystals dominates it.

Process-history dependence

Final temperature alone was not sufficient to predict the outcome. Batch 6 first crystallized at 298 K, reheated to 303 K, held, and recooled to 300 K. It retained recovery 0.358 but had fines 1.000 and d50 about 18 micrometres. Batch 7 used a stronger 310 K reheat after the 298 K excursion and still ended with recovery 0.383 and fines 0.983. I infer that the initial deep-cooling event created a large fine-particle population that the reheating steps did not fully dissolve; subsequent cooling then regrew or regenerated that population. This interpretation is more consistent with the results than an equilibrium-only solubility model.

Seeding also depended on supersaturation history. Increasing the seed charge alone did not prevent fines after deep cooling: batch 9 used about 1 g of seed and cooled to 298 K, yet recovered 0.393 with fines 0.972. Conversely, direct operation near 300–301 K with about 2 g of seed preserved a seed-dominated coarse population. Batch 11, held only 1,800 s at 300 K, showed essentially zero seed-excluded recovery, fines 0.000086, and d50 about 98 micrometres. Extending the corresponding hold to 7,200 s in batch 12 raised recovery to 0.00836 while retaining purity 1.000, fines reported as 0, and d50 about 106 micrometres. This suggests an induction/growth period near 300 K, followed by a likely nucleation cliff if supersaturation or residence time is increased too far.

Recommended batch and unresolved tradeoff

The sealed recommendation remains batch 12 because it had the greatest measured seed-excluded recovery among batches satisfying both purity ≥0.80 and fines ≤0.50. Its measured recovery was 0.00836, purity 1.000, fines 0, normalized size 0.4245, and CSD quality 0.9897. It did not reach the 0.10 feasibility target. The campaign therefore found two regimes rather than a fully satisfactory optimum: a high-recovery/fine-particle regime and a coarse, specification-compliant/very-low-recovery regime.

Revisions and uncertainty

The initial approach emphasized deep cooling for recovery, but batches 1–2 revealed severe fines. Warm-endpoint trials then established that coarse seed-dominated solids were possible, while batches 6–7 tested and rejected simple thermal cycling as a sufficient cure for fines formed during an earlier deep-cooling excursion. Larger seed charges in batches 9, 11, and 12 showed that seeding helps only when the process avoids the deep-supersaturation nucleation regime.

These conclusions are uncertain because most conditions were tested once, catalyst comparisons were confounded with temperature and time, and final-assay noise is material relative to the very small compliant recoveries. Reported zeros may also reflect clipping/noise rather than exact physical zeros. Particle-size readings before filtration and final-assay values were broadly consistent in regime classification, but not exact replicates. Untested possibilities include a finely resolved temperature window between 300 and 301 K, gentler continuous ramps, removal immediately after limited growth, alternative agitation histories, or a designed factorial study separating catalyst, temperature, seed surface area, and crystallization residence time. Such approaches might locate an intermediate state with recovery above 0.10 before secondary nucleation dominates, but the completed campaign provides no direct evidence that this window exists.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- Near-complete conversion made selectivity a major upstream limitation. Batch 1 had conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.534 and reaction yield 0.531; the C3/S2 batches similarly had roughly 0.99–1.00 conversion and reaction yields around 0.54. The interpretation that selectivity controls available target is therefore reasonable, although the approximate relation yield ≈ conversion × selectivity is not exact.
- Crystallization usually rejected impurities effectively. Meaningful-recovery batches 1, 4, 6–9 had crystal purities of about 0.95–1.00 despite appreciable reaction byproduct signals. Preferential target crystallization is an interpretation; the high measured purities themselves are observations.
- A strong recovery–particle-quality tradeoff was directly observed. Batch 4 recovered 0.368 but had fines 1.000, whereas batches 5 and 10 had fines near zero and coarse particles but recoveries of only 0.00735 and 0.00656. Batch 12 was likewise coarse and compliant but recovered only 0.00836.
- Deep supersaturation overwhelmed increased seeding. Batch 9 used about 1 g of seed yet, after cooling to 298 K, still produced recovery 0.393 with fines 0.972. This directly contradicts a simple claim that more seed alone suppresses secondary nucleation.
- Once a fine population formed, the tested reheating cycles did not remove it. Batch 6 crystallized at 298 K, reheated to 303 K and recooled, but ended with fines 1.000. Batch 7 used a 310 K reheat and still had fines 0.983. Persistence or regeneration of nuclei is an interpretation, but failure of these cycles to restore quality is directly observed.

Partly supported but confounded:
- C3 appeared robust in the tested S2 region, with batches 4–12 commonly giving reaction yields near 0.54. C0 and C2 were poorer in batches 2 and 3. Catalyst identity, temperature and residence time were changed together, however, so catalyst superiority was not isolated.
- S2 appeared preferable to S3: batch 8 with S3 had reaction yield 0.465 versus approximately 0.54 for nearby C3/S2 batches, without improving fines. This comparison is directionally useful but not clean because crystallization temperatures and histories differed.
- Batches 11 and 12 support some time dependence near 300 K: extending the direct hold from 1,800 to 7,200 s increased recovery from approximately zero to 0.00836 while retaining coarse particles. Two endpoints do not establish whether this is ordinary seed growth, an induction period, or proximity to an equilibrium solubility limit.

Contradicted or revised:
- The nominal low nucleation tendency and high growth tendency of S2 did not guarantee a coarse product under deep cooling; batches 1, 4, 6, 7 and 9 all generated excessive fines.
- Simple thermal ripening was not an effective remedy under the tested cycles, as shown by batches 6 and 7.
- Large seed mass was not sufficient under strong supersaturation, as shown by batch 9.

Still untested:
- Whether a narrow temperature/time window between the coarse, low-recovery regime and the fine, high-recovery regime can exceed 0.10 recovery while satisfying the fines limit.
- Clean factorial catalyst and solvent effects at identical reaction and crystallization conditions.
- Whether controlled agitation, a genuinely gradual ramp, or removal at a precisely chosen induction time could suppress secondary nucleation.
- Whether the apparent transition is primarily an equilibrium-solubility cliff, a kinetic induction phenomenon, or a nucleation avalanche.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the batch-12 upstream recipe and seed charge, cool directly to 300 K, but extend the isothermal crystallization to 14,400 s. I would take non-destructive particle-size readings at approximately 1,800, 7,200 and 14,400 s, then filter and obtain one final assay. This extends the existing batch-11/batch-12 time series without changing temperature, seed loading or upstream chemistry.

It would distinguish three explanations:
- Equilibrium-limited regime: recovery would remain near 0.01 even after 14,400 s, with normalized size near 0.4 and low fines. The sharp difference from 298 K would then mainly reflect solubility.
- Seed-growth-limited regime: seed-excluded recovery would rise progressively, potentially above 0.10, while particles remained coarse and fines stayed at or below 0.50. This would reveal the desired operating window.
- Delayed nucleation avalanche: early measurements would remain coarse, followed by a rapid decrease in size and rise in fines; final recovery might approach 0.3–0.4 but fines would exceed 0.9. This would support the high-order nucleation interpretation.

3. Least-used observation and least-reliable prediction

The account used the paired pre-filtration particle-size measurements and final-assay CSD values least effectively. For example, batch 7 changed from a pre-filtration normalized size of 0.061 with fines 1.000 to a final-assay size of 0.025 with fines 0.983; batch 9 changed from size 0.045/fines 1.000 to size 0.0157/fines 0.972. I treated these as the same qualitative regime, but their quantitative disagreement should have been used more explicitly to separate sampling and instrument uncertainty from true filtration or slurry-history effects. It limits confidence in precise CSD kinetics even when the coarse-versus-fine classification is clear.

Q11 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It extrapolates simultaneously to solvent S1, a lower reagent loading, a much smaller catalyst-to-reagent ratio, and a 385 K reaction—conditions not directly represented in the campaign. Its predicted fines estimate of 0.72 also had an 80% interval of 0.38–0.94, crossing the 0.50 feasibility boundary. Consequently, both its particle regime and its sealed quality-feasible classification are much less secure than predictions lying clearly in the high-fines regime.

payload.rationale: Identical recipes receive identical predictions: Q01/Q03/Q05 and Q07/Q10. For the solvent pair, S3 is expected to improve impurity rejection and intrinsic growth/nucleation balance relative to S1, but its lower solubility and weaker reaction activity offset this with deeper supersaturation and slightly lower recovery. Increasing seed from 0.006 to 0.05 g should enlarge particles and reduce fines modestly, but prior batches showed that seed loading cannot suppress secondary nucleation under deep cooling. Staged cooling is expected to be less damaging than an immediate 278.15 K excursion, so Q06 has the smallest particles and most fines. Reheating in Q08 may dissolve some fines, but campaign thermal-cycle batches showed strong history persistence and renewed nucleation on recooling. An additional low-temperature growth period raises recovery slightly in Q10 versus Q09 but is more likely to generate secondary fines than to ripen them. Lower upstream loading in Q11 reduces supersaturation, sacrificing recovery while giving the only material chance of approaching the fines limit; higher loading in Q12 does the reverse. All batches are seeded and therefore should contain particles. Purity is likely acceptable throughout, but the estimated fines fractions make every central prediction quality-infeasible. Intervals represent model uncertainty in transferring from the campaign to substantially different charge, catalyst loading, solvent, and thermal conditions, not final-assay measurement noise.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 had the highest measured seed-excluded crystal yield among batches meeting both quality constraints (purity 1.000 and fines 0.000), but its yield was only 0.00836, so no quality-compliant batch reached the 0.10 feasibility target.
